newsitem.title: USA: Miami woes not affecting area's tourism - mayor.
newsitem.headline: Miami woes not affecting area's tourism - mayor.

text.p: The mayor of Florida's Dade County sought to reassure potential visitors on Thursday that Miami's financial mess has not affected the larger metropolitan area and its tourism-dependent economy.

The city has a $68 million budget deficit which on Tuesday forced Florida Governor Lawton Chiles to declare a financial emergency and appoint a panel to oversee the city's recovery from its crippling mismanagement.
That led Dade County Mayor Alex Penelas to try to distance his jursidiction from the impoverished city while offering financial aid and expertise to help get Miami get on track.

"I'm very concerned with the national and international headlines. For the national and international community, there is no difference between Miami and Miami Beach and Dade County," Penelas said. "The city of Miami is our flagship city and we all suffer from the consequences."

Miami is the Dade County seat but only one of 29 independent municipalities in a sprawling conurbation. The Miami urban area has more than two million residents in two dozen cities, of which only 365,000 people live in Miami city.

Penelas called a news conference to announce the county would help the city by continuing to offer a $10 million loan first discussed in October, and by offering to buy some prime, city-owned waterfront land earmarked for a sports arena.
The mayor said the county, which has already loaned a dozen budget executives to the city, was prepared to provide police and other services if the city was forced to cut back.

"We stand committed to help the city of Miami through its problems. This financial crisis is serious but it is also manageable," Penelas said. But he expressed concern that Miami's fiscal disgrace would deter visitors, crippling the county's $8.5 billion tourism industry.
Miami International Airport, the Port of Miami, the public hospital and the tourist police programme are all run by the county and are unaffected by Miami's budget crunch, he said.

Tourism and business officials said Miami's woes had so far not hurt the area's economy. "Businesses are continuing to look at Miami as a viable location for their headquarters," Carol Wyllie, head of an economic development group, said.
Robert Beatty of the Greater Miami Visitors and Convention Bureau said, "1996 was a banner year for the tourism industry. Even with these problems we expect 1997 to be even better."
While Miami's credit rating was cut to non-investment grade, or "junk" status, Dade county's general obligation debt is rated A-1 by Moody's Investor Service and A-plus by Standard & Poor's Corp.
